No slides were found for this lecture. The page is built from the doctor's notes (green) and every gift (red). Aldughaither's summaries have no lower-GI-bleeding, colonic diverticular or angiodysplasia chapter, so there is no grey section here.

General approach

StepWhat it involves
HistoryCharacter of bleeding, painful vs painless, anticoagulants, NSAIDs, prior episodes, screening history
ExaminationFull abdominal assessment
DREPart of the examination, not optional — always assess local/perianal causes
Labs + adjunctsLabs, imaging, endoscopy — chosen by the differential
ImpressionDifferential → top differential → targeted investigations
  • Investigations must be judicious and tailored to what you're ruling in or out. The small bowel accounts for only ~5% of GI bleeding — a diagnosis of exclusion after upper and colonic sources.
  • Landmark separating upper from lower GI bleeding → duodenojejunal junction (ligament of Treitz). 434 ×2

Blood appearance

AppearanceSuggests
Bright redFresh/distal source — haemorrhoids, rectal or distal colonic lesions
Darker, mixed with stoolMore proximal (longer in the bowel)
MelenaUpper GI or small bowel
Fresh or clottedLeft-sided colon can give either
  • Ask: fresh or dark? liquid or clotted? melena? mixed with stool? Colour is an indicator, not a rule — haemorrhoidal blood can clot in the rectum.

Massive haematochezia — don't miss an upper GI source

Massive haematochezia with haemodynamic compromise → always consider a brisk upper GI bleed. History → exam → DRE → upper endoscopy (or NG assessment) → no upper source → colonoscopy → still not found → CTA / tagged RBC scan / catheter angiography.
  • Bleeding per rectum with a normal colonoscopy → next upper GI endoscopy to exclude an upper source. 426

Diverticular disease — one lesion, two diseases

  • A diverticulum = mucosal/submucosal outpouching through a weak point where the vessels penetrate the colonic wall — which explains both complications.
Diverticular bleedingDiverticulitis
MechanismVessel (vasa recta) rupturesInflammation/perforation
SideMore often the RIGHT colonUsually SIGMOID / left colon
PresentationPainless, sudden, can be massive; often self-limited, may re-bleedLLQ pain, fever, malaise
Frequency~⅓ of all acute LGIB~75% uncomplicated
LGIB?Most common cause of acute LGIBNot a typical cause of LGIB
SurgerySubtotal colectomySegmental sigmoidectomy
Diverticular bleeding is NOT diverticulitis — same diverticula, different side, presentation and operation.
  • Background: ~50% have diverticulosis by age 60; few become symptomatic; constipation/low-fibre diet; right-sided disease more common in Asians.

Diverticular bleeding

  • Most common cause of acute LGIB (~⅓); painless, sudden, potentially massive; often self-limited. Short-term recurrence ~50%; lifetime recurrence 15–25% without resection. Always ask about anticoagulants/NSAIDs.
  • Significant acute LGIB: resuscitate first, investigate second — vitals, IV access, IV fluids, Hb, NPO, transfusion when indicated. A stable clinic patient doesn't need emergency resuscitation.
  • Elderly woman, painless rectal bleeding, stable, similar attacks before → diverticulosis 426; painless massive rectal bleeding, NG aspirate bile without blood → diverticulosis. 431
  • Massive painless haematochezia, diverticula everywhere but none bleeding at colonoscopy → source → vasa recta. 442

Localising the bleed

ModalityDetectsRoleTreats?
1. Colonoscopy—Usually the initial test after stabilisation; finds the source, excludes cancer/anorectal causes; bleeding often stopped by thenYes — adrenaline injection, thermal, clips
2. CT angiography≈ 0.3 mL/minWhen colonoscopy can't localise; non-invasive, highly accurateNo
3. Catheter angiography≈ 0.5 mL/minInvasive, least sensitive, but therapeuticYes — embolization
4. Tagged RBC scan≈ 0.1 mL/minMost sensitive for slow bleeding but ~25% false localisationNo
All localisation tests need active bleeding. Never embolize an unlocalised vessel (bowel ischaemia) — localise first, then treat.
  • Most useful imaging to localise active lower GI bleeding → CT angiography (stable/inactive → colonoscopy). 435 ×5

Surgery for uncontrolled diverticular bleeding

  • When: source can't be controlled or localised · persistent major bleeding despite resuscitation · ~4–6 units PRBC in 24 h · bleeding for ~72 h.
Operation: total abdominal (subtotal) colectomy, rectum preserved (ileorectal anastomosis or ileostomy) — ~25% mortality. Avoid a segmental resection for unlocalised bleeding (re-bleeding from the colon left behind). The rectum is spared because the taeniae coli converge there (no diverticula).
  • Same woman collapses, SBP 80 despite transfusion → transfusion + laparotomy + total colectomy. 426
  • Follow-up: no routine serial colonoscopy for diverticulosis; counsel about recurrence. Screening colonoscopy from age 45; normal → repeat ~10 years.

Diverticulitis

  • Uncomplicated = no abscess, perforation, fistula or stricture/obstruction (~75%). Complicated = any one of them.
  • Presentation: LLQ pain, fever, malaise (right-sided possible, more in Asians). Labs: leukocytosis, ↑ CRP, ↑ ESR. Definitive test: CT abdomen. History, exam and DRE first.
HincheyFindingImplication
0UncomplicatedNon-operative if stable
ISmall/localised pericolic abscessOften non-operative
IILarger, distant or pelvic abscessOften non-operative (drainage)
IIIPurulent peritonitisGenerally surgery
IVFaecal peritonitisSurgery
ScenarioManagement
Abscess < 3 cm (stable)IV antibiotics + supportive (too small to drain)
Abscess > 3 cm (stable)IR percutaneous drainage + IV antibiotics
BothIV access, hydration, bowel rest, admission
Straight to ORInstability, peritonitis, free perforation, Hinchey III–IV
The abscess is the one complication that can be talked out of surgery. Fistula, stricture/obstruction and major perforation usually need surgery.
  • Colonoscopy after diverticulitis — once inflammation resolves, never during it (perforation). Occult cancer risk ≈ 11% after complicated vs ≈ 1% after uncomplicated.
  • Elective surgery: segmental (sigmoid) resection, decided by quality of life — not age or a fixed number of attacks.
  • Elderly man, bleeding with diarrhoea, LIF pain, thick sigmoid on X-ray → fluids and antibiotics. 428

Angiodysplasia

  • Dilated submucosal vascular lesion with a feeding vessel — right colon, elderly. Incidental in ~2% of colonoscopies; only ~15% bleed significantly. Bleeding usually slow and intermittent → iron-deficiency anaemia. Treatment: endoscopic (injection, thermal/bipolar, clips); surgery rarely. Asymptomatic incidental lesions → leave alone.
  • 70-year-old, massive fresh PR bleeding without pain, shocked, NG drains green fluid → keyed angiodysplasia 434 ×2; massive PR bleeding, Hb 6, shocked → angiodysplasia. 429
  • Angiodysplasia with massive bleeding, unstable → angiographic embolization (surgery if it fails). 427 429 ×3

Colitis

  • Colitis usually causes smaller-volume bleeding (UC can give heavy bloody diarrhoea): IBD, ischaemic, radiation, infectious.

Ischaemic colitis vs mesenteric ischaemia

Ischaemic colitisMesenteric ischaemia
OrganColonPrimarily small bowel
MechanismCommonly non-occlusive / low-flow (elderly, sick, dehydrated)Commonly arterial occlusion/embolism (AF)
TerritoryWatershed — splenic flexureArterial distribution
UrgencyOften improves with IV fluids, NPO, antibioticsTrue emergency
  • Elderly diabetic, LLQ pain, bloody diarrhoea, fever, leukocytosis, thumb-printing of descending/sigmoid colon → ischaemic colitis 434 ×3; thumbprint sign → ischaemic colitis. 434

Infectious colitis & IBD

  • Bloody diarrhoea (inflamed mucosa can't absorb water) → stool culture; E. coli, Campylobacter, Shigella; treat the infection.
  • 10–15 episodes of bloody diarrhoea, dehydrated, hypotensive, cachectic → admit and rehydrate with IV fluids 437 436 ×2
  • Fever, 6 bloody stools, leukocytosis, generalized tenderness → keyed colectomy. 427
  • Recurrent fistula, bloody mucus, tenesmus, unhealthy rectum → keyed Crohn's or UC (fistula favours Crohn's; rectal involvement and bloody mucus favour UC). 427
  • Young woman with IBD (mild colitis a year ago), now haematochezia → Crohn's flare (or CRC — colitis raises cancer risk). 441

Other causes (from past exams)

  • 70-year-old: bright red blood mixed with stool, constipation, weight loss, pale → colon cancer. 436 ×6
  • Haematochezia with 3rd-degree haemorrhoids in a 62-year-old → colonoscopy first (> 45) 436 ×2; 20-year-old with haemorrhoids but family history of colon cancer and iron-deficiency anaemia → colonoscopy. 439 ×2
  • Painful bright red bleeding, worst during and after defecation → anal fissure 430 ×2 429 ×2
